title: The Line That Reveals Judas Was Drifting Long Before Betrayal
paragraphs:
The Line That Reveals Judas Was Drifting Long Before Betrayal
The sentence most people skip may explain how hearts slowly walk away from Jesus before anyone notices.
Most people think Judas became Judas in a single night.

A kiss.
Thirty pieces of silver.
A garden.
A betrayal.
That is usually where the story begins in our minds.
But Scripture tells a far more terrifying story.
Judas did not fall in one night.
He drifted.
And the most frightening part is that almost nobody around him seemed to notice.
He still walked with Jesus.
He still heard the sermons.
He still witnessed miracles.
He still traveled with the disciples.
He still looked like one of them.
Yet beneath the surface, something was slowly dying.
That reality should shake every believer because it reveals a truth many Christians do not want to confront:
It is possible to be physically close to Jesus while your heart is quietly moving away from Him.
The line that exposes Judas' condition appears long before the betrayal.
It appears in John 12.
Mary had entered the room carrying an alabaster jar filled with costly perfume. She broke it and poured it upon Jesus.
The fragrance filled the house.
It was a moment of extravagant worship.
But Judas saw something different.
Scripture records his response:
“Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” (John 12:5)
At first glance, it sounds spiritual.
Compassionate.
Responsible.
Even noble.
But then John reveals what was actually happening.
"He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief; and having the money box, he used to take what was put into it." (John 12:6)
The Greek word John uses is κλέπτης (kleptēs).
Not merely someone tempted by greed.
A thief.
A taker.
Someone who secretly steals.
Notice what happened.
Judas criticized worship because his heart had already begun loving something else.
Before he betrayed Jesus publicly, he had already betrayed Him privately.
Long before the kiss, there was compromise.
Long before the silver, there was secret theft.
Long before the scandal, there was drift.
That is how spiritual collapse often works.
The world imagines people wake up one day and abandon God.
Scripture reveals something different.
Hearts usually leave long before bodies do.
The betrayal simply exposes what has already been growing in secret.
That is why Jesus repeatedly warned about the condition of the heart.
Not appearances.
Not performance.
Not reputation.
The heart.
The Hebrew Scriptures often use the word לֵב (lev), meaning the inner person—the seat of desire, affection, will, and devotion.
God was never primarily after external behavior.
He was after the lev.
The heart.
Because whatever captures the heart eventually directs the life.
Judas' problem was not ultimately money.
Money was simply the symptom.
His real problem was misplaced worship.
He wanted Jesus close enough to benefit him but not close enough to rule him.
And if we are honest, many of us understand that struggle more than we want to admit.
Some people have not abandoned church.
But they have abandoned intimacy with Christ.
Some still sing worship songs.
But their minds are somewhere else.
Some still post Bible verses.
But secret compromises have begun taking root beneath the surface.
Some still look faithful to everyone around them.
Yet inside they are drifting.
Quietly.
Gradually.
Dangerously.
That is why Judas' story remains so unsettling.
We see pieces of ourselves in it.
Not because we want to betray Jesus.
But because we know how easy it is for other loves to slowly compete with Him.
Success.
Money.
Comfort.
Relationships.
Status.
Approval.
Control.
The drift rarely begins with rebellion.
It usually begins with distraction.
One small compromise.
One secret habit.
One neglected prayer life.
One ignored conviction.
One postponed act of obedience.
Until eventually the distance becomes greater than we ever intended.
Yet the story of Scripture is not ultimately about Judas.
It is about Jesus.
Because while Judas reveals the tragedy of a drifting heart, Jesus reveals the relentless love of God toward sinners.
Even knowing Judas would betray Him, Jesus still washed his feet.
Think about that.
The Son of God knelt before the man who would sell Him.
Jesus knew.
Yet He served him anyway.
That is grace.
Not sentimental grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not permissive grace.
Grace that loves sinners while fully knowing their condition.
Grace that exposes darkness so healing can begin.
Grace that calls wandering hearts home.
The Gospel is not merely the story of how bad Judas became.
The Gospel is the story of how good Jesus remains.
Even when we drift.
Even when we fail.
Even when we fall.
The Greek word often translated grace is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of unearned favor.
A gift that cannot be purchased.
A kindness that originates in God's character rather than our performance.
That means your hope is not found in your ability to hold onto Christ.
Your ultimate hope is found in Christ holding onto you.
The warning of Judas should lead us to examination.
But the love of Jesus should lead us to repentance.
If there is drift, return.
If there is compromise, confess it.
If there is distance, come home.
Because the same Savior who exposed Judas' heart is still inviting people into forgiveness today.
And perhaps that is why this story continues to grip us after two thousand years.
It is not merely about a disciple who fell.
It is about every human heart that has ever wandered.
It is about every believer who has ever felt the pull of competing loves.
It is about every person who wonders whether grace can still reach them.
And the answer of the Gospel remains the same.
Yes.
Jesus still saves.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still rewrites stories.
Maybe that is why you found yourself reading this far.
Not because this article is about Judas.
But because somewhere deep inside, you recognized that drift can happen to anyone.
Be honest.
Has your heart become distracted?
Has worship become routine?
Has intimacy with Jesus been replaced by religious activity?
Has something else quietly taken first place?
If the Holy Spirit is revealing something, do not ignore Him.
Return while your heart is still tender.
Return while His invitation is still being extended.
Return because grace is still available.
The most dangerous betrayals are not the ones that happen in a moment—they are the ones that begin when a heart slowly stops being amazed by Jesus.
